_comment: Frozen vocabulary for the coordination board. The GUI (mycelium-frontend/src/lib/board/) and the CLI (mycelium-cli/src/mycelium/board/) each carry their own copy of the projection rules — the thin `uv tool` CLI can't import the frontend and vice versa — so the words they must agree on live here, the same way contracts/slim-l9-wire.json freezes the SLIM+L9 constants. A unit test on each side asserts against this file, so neither copy can drift without a red gate.
_row_actions_comment: Two kinds of action, and the split is the point. A ROW ACTION changes the row: its assignment through the lease endpoints, everything else as frontmatter. A CHAT verb (`chat_verbs`) changes nothing about the row and says something in the thread the row is — the room's own chat verbs (`room send` / `room messages`) with a row id in front of them, one transport (mycelium-cli/src/mycelium/chat.py) rather than a second implementation that would drift on attribution. The two lists are asserted DISJOINT. `new` is a row action with nothing to mutate yet — board-first creation, the only way a task gets its thread minted — so it takes no keystroke and is absent from row_action_keys.

task._comment: A task is a board row and a thread: one row per task, with its coordination folded into it. The binding is `binding_field` on the row's memory — store-owned, minted by the backend, carried across writes, so it is absent from the meta bag a caller can write and a field write cannot move a row onto someone else's thread. The thread's own state lands under `thread_fields` because a task's status and assignment are the task's: a negotiation that converges or aborts inside a row must not resolve the row or take it off its holder, which is what `task_fields` names — the container-outlives-the-negotiation rule, as a list both sides assert a fold against. An episode no row is bound to is an ORPHAN: it keeps its own row rather than being hidden or deleted, which is why the board still projects episodes.
task._refusals_comment: Why a row has no thread to speak into, keyed by the source that produced it. A chat verb refuses in these terms rather than falling back to the room: a message that quietly went somewhere other than where it was addressed is worse than one that did not go. Keyed by source kind, so an episode row is absent — an episode IS a thread, and speaking into a recorded negotiation is a write the hub judges (a frozen roster refuses an outsider), not one the surface guesses at. The memory refusal is no longer about namespace: EVERY memory a person authored carries a thread, board namespace or not (#872), so the only unthreaded memory left is one the hub wrote for itself — an agents/ manifest, a log/ record, context/synthesis.

refusals.agent: presence is a lease the runtime renews, not a conversation to join
refusals.memory: the hub writes this memory for itself; a thread belongs to something a person authored

log._comment: The daily log's calendar conventions. A day is a calendar date in the reader's timezone; weeks start Monday; the heat scale steps at these upper bounds.

upstream._comment: What a status provider's answer looks like on a row. The field is `upstream` and not `status` (the row's own lifecycle) or `live` (a boolean for whether an agent is resident on the row): a provider answers about the work upstream of this room, in the tool it actually lives in. States are ordered worst first, which is the order a row with two references picks by. `companion_fields` is every other key the two implementations write, and both assert this list against what they actually produce rather than against a copy of it.

assignment._comment: Assignment: who holds a row, and for how much longer. Separate from `status` because an ephemeral actor cannot promise the future — every claim it makes runs on a window, so the board must be able to say a holder went quiet without anyone writing that down. `held` is the only state with a holder; `unclaimed` and `expired` are derived and never stored, which is why `stored_states` is the shorter list. Freshness is the same shape the upstream model already ships (fresh/stale/expired against fetched_at/ttl), pointed at claimed_at. The word is `assignment` and not `custody`: `custody` is taken, by the hub holding a member's MLS keys (fastapi-backend/app/services/custody.py), which shares no concept with this.

refusals.episode: an episode is a recorded negotiation, and there is nothing to assign
refusals.agent: presence is already a lease the runtime renews; it is not claimable
refusals.memory: assignments live on work/ memories; this row is in another namespace

fields._comment: What a row action writes when it is not an assignment: frontmatter on the row's memory, through the same upsert `memory set --meta` goes through. Only a memory carries frontmatter, so every other projected row refuses in its own terms rather than accepting a write that goes nowhere. The reserved set is deliberately NOT listed here — it is derived from `assignment` (its field, its companion fields, and the holder), and each implementation asserts that derivation rather than a second copy that could drift.

refusals.episode: an episode is a recorded negotiation, not a row the room can edit
refusals.agent: presence is what the runtime reports, not a field you set
refusals.capture: this row is not in the room yet; capture it first
refusals.github: this value belongs to the tool it came from; change it there

schema._comment: Field types the two surfaces must infer identically, and the order options come back in. `cases` is a table both suites run through their own classifier: a field name, the values it holds, and the type both must call it. These drifted once (the GUI grew number-from-string and link rules the CLI never got, and sorted out-of-vocabulary options first where the CLI sorted them last), which is what a table asserted from both sides prevents.
